rawInterpretation: I will probably lose my job.
alternateRealityChecks: Organisational changes can affect roles in many different ways.
Restructuring does not automatically result in job loss.
No information has specifically indicated that your role is affected.
The future is currently uncertain rather than predetermined.
revisedInterpretation: There may be changes ahead, but I do not have evidence that my job is at risk.
chosenBehaviour: Stay informed and focus on factors within my control.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Leadership shared additional details and my role was unchanged.

event: A colleague with similar experience was promoted before me.
rawInterpretation: My career is falling behind everyone else's.
alternateRealityChecks: Promotions depend on multiple factors beyond tenure.
Career progression is rarely linear.
One person's advancement does not determine your future opportunities.
Comparisons often ignore differences in circumstances and goals.
revisedInterpretation: Their promotion does not define the trajectory of my career.
outcomeOneWeekLater: My manager outlined potential opportunities for advancement.

event: I am considering changing careers but feel unsure.
rawInterpretation: If I switch careers, I will probably regret it.
alternateRealityChecks: Future outcomes cannot be known with certainty.
Career decisions can often be tested gradually.
Many people successfully transition careers multiple times.
Regret is only one of several possible outcomes.
revisedInterpretation: The decision involves uncertainty, but I can explore options before committing.
chosenBehaviour: Research the field and speak with people already working in it.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I gained useful insights through informational conversations.

event: Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of tasks in my profession.
rawInterpretation: My skills will become completely obsolete.
alternateRealityChecks: Technology often changes jobs rather than eliminating them entirely.
New tools also create opportunities and new skill requirements.
Adaptability is an important professional strength.
The future impact is uncertain and likely more nuanced than complete replacement.
revisedInterpretation: My profession may evolve, but adaptation remains possible.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I identified training opportunities relevant to future trends.

event: I received a job rejection after several interview rounds.
rawInterpretation: I am not good enough for the jobs I want.
alternateRealityChecks: One hiring decision does not define your ability.
Hiring outcomes depend on many factors beyond competence.
Reaching later interview stages suggests strengths were recognised.
Future opportunities remain available.
revisedInterpretation: The rejection is disappointing but does not define my professional value.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I received invitations to additional interviews.

event: My work feels repetitive compared to what my peers are doing.
rawInterpretation: I am wasting my career potential.
alternateRealityChecks: Repeating work can still build important expertise.
Career growth often includes periods of stability.
Peer experiences may look different from the outside than they feel internally.
One phase does not define an entire career.
revisedInterpretation: I may be ready for new challenges, but that does not mean my current experience lacks value.
chosenBehaviour: Explore development opportunities within my role.
outcomeOneWeekLater: A new project opportunity became available.

event: I am considering returning to school later in my career.
rawInterpretation: I am too old to make such a change.
alternateRealityChecks: People begin new educational paths at many different ages.
Experience can be an advantage in learning.
Age alone does not determine success.
There are many examples of successful later-career transitions.
revisedInterpretation: The decision deserves thoughtful consideration, but age alone is not a reason to avoid it.
chosenBehaviour: Research programmes and speak with mature students.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I discovered several flexible learning options.

event: I have not figured out my long-term career path.
rawInterpretation: Everyone else knows exactly where they are going except me.
alternateRealityChecks: Many people experience uncertainty about their long-term direction.
Career paths often emerge through experimentation rather than planning.
People frequently appear more certain externally than they actually feel.
Not having all the answers today is normal.
revisedInterpretation: Career uncertainty is common and does not indicate failure.
chosenBehaviour: Focus on the next useful step rather than the entire path.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I identified several areas I wanted to explore further.

event: A role I wanted was given to an external candidate.
rawInterpretation: The company does not see potential in me.
alternateRealityChecks: External candidates may bring specialised experience.
One staffing decision does not reflect all perceptions of your ability.
Hiring decisions often involve multiple business considerations.
The decision provides limited information about your future opportunities.
revisedInterpretation: The hiring outcome does not necessarily reflect how my potential is viewed.
chosenBehaviour: Discuss future opportunities and expectations with leadership.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I learned more about the specific skills required for the role.

event: I am considering starting a business but feel uncertain about the risks.
rawInterpretation: If I fail, it will ruin my career.
alternateRealityChecks: Career setbacks are often recoverable.
Many entrepreneurs learn from unsuccessful ventures.
There are ways to test ideas before committing fully.
Failure is not the only possible outcome.
revisedInterpretation: The decision involves risk, but it is unlikely that one outcome would permanently define my career.
chosenBehaviour: Evaluate options gradually and manage risks realistically.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I created a plan to test the idea on a small scale.

event: Several projects have recently been cancelled and leadership has spoken about reducing costs.
rawInterpretation: Layoffs are definitely coming and I will be affected.
alternateRealityChecks: The recent events suggest there may be organisational challenges.
Cost reduction can take many forms besides layoffs.
There is currently no specific evidence that your role will be affected.
It is reasonable to prepare for uncertainty without assuming a specific outcome.
revisedInterpretation: The situation creates uncertainty, but I do not have enough information to conclude that I will lose my job.
chosenBehaviour: Update my resume and stay informed while continuing to perform well.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Leadership clarified that spending controls were being introduced but no workforce changes were announced.

event: I have been in the same role for four years and have not yet received a promotion.
alternateRealityChecks: A slower promotion timeline does not determine the rest of your career.
Career progression often occurs in cycles rather than at a constant pace.
Promotion depends on multiple factors including organisational opportunities.
Current progress does not predict future progress with certainty.
revisedInterpretation: I may need to understand what is required for advancement, but my career is not permanently stalled.
chosenBehaviour: Discuss promotion expectations and growth opportunities with my manager.
outcomeOneWeekLater: A development plan was created with measurable goals.

event: My industry is changing rapidly and many new skills are becoming important.
rawInterpretation: I will never be able to keep up with these changes.
alternateRealityChecks: No professional learns every new skill immediately.
Most successful careers involve continuous learning over time.
You can prioritise the skills most relevant to your goals.
The challenge is gradual adaptation, not instant mastery.
revisedInterpretation: The industry is evolving, but I can adapt by learning incrementally.
chosenBehaviour: Create a focused learning plan for the next six months.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I identified several high-impact skills and learning resources.

event: I received feedback that my current skillset may not fully match the direction of future projects.
rawInterpretation: I am becoming irrelevant and will eventually be replaced.
alternateRealityChecks: The feedback identifies a genuine development opportunity.
Skill gaps can often be addressed through training and experience.
Many organisations provide time and support for upskilling.
Needing additional skills does not imply replacement is inevitable.
revisedInterpretation: There is a legitimate need to expand my skillset, but I am not automatically at risk of becoming irrelevant.
chosenBehaviour: Invest in learning skills aligned with future work.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Relevant training opportunities were identified and approved.

event: I no longer feel motivated or fulfilled by my current work.
rawInterpretation: I chose the wrong career and have wasted years of my life.
alternateRealityChecks: A period of dissatisfaction does not invalidate previous experiences.
Career interests naturally evolve over time.
The skills and experiences gained remain valuable regardless of future choices.
Feeling unfulfilled may indicate a need for change, not that past decisions were mistakes.
revisedInterpretation: My current role may no longer meet my needs, but my past experience still has value and can inform future decisions.
chosenBehaviour: Reflect on what is missing and explore alternative career paths.
outcomeOneWeekLater: I gained clarity about the type of work I want to pursue in the future.
